fact: Gamtel states it is connected to the ACE (Africa Coast to Europe) submarine fibre cable, with three international gateways totalling 15 Gbps at the time of the page.
Gamtel states two international routes: the ACE submarine cable and a 155 Mbps backup link with Sonatel in Senegal; landing station not named in this document (page date used, as it gives no other).

The Point reports, citing an unnamed source, that the ACE submarine cable station in Sukuta is the facility connecting The Gambia to international internet networks and lost power on 4 June 2026, causing a nationwide outage; a temporary outage, not a route loss.
The ACE consortium states the ACE cable was first put into service on 15 December 2012, is the first international submarine cable to land in Gambia, and lists Banjul as a landing station.
TechGriot reports The Gambia remains structurally dependent on a single undersea cable, the ACE submarine cable, with terrestrial redundancy through Senegal still thin.

WBBA case study says the ACE submarine cable's first-mile network is in service in Gambia, with GAMTEL's ECOWAN and NBN backbones; it reports international bandwidth rising from 10 Gbps in 2015 to 220+ Gbps in 2020-2022. Document is undated; published date 2024-05 used.

GAMTEL says it is connected to the ACE (Africa Coast to Europe) cable through 4 separate international gateways, with 25,000 Megabit capacity from Portugal and France Telecoms; no landing station is named. The page is undated, so the date is its capture date.

GAMTEL states two international routes in service: the ACE cable, and a 28 Gbps backup link with Free (Senegal) on Cross Gambia (CG2) to which traffic is automatically rerouted if ACE fails; no landing station or border point is named. The page is undated, so the date is its capture date.
